Sociologists and their Famous Statements/Theories:

INDIAN SOCIOLOGISTS

Sociologist Famous Statement / Theory M. N. Srinivas Sanskritization, Westernization, Dominant Caste G. S. Ghurye "Caste is characterized by segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on

feeding and social intercourse." Irawati Karve "Kinship is the backbone of Indian social organization." A. R. Desai Nationalism emerged from socio-economic changes under colonialism. Yogendra Singh Modernization of Indian Tradition Andre Beteille Relationship among Caste, Class and Power N. K. Bose Change in India occurs through adjustment rather than conflict. D. P. Mukerji Tradition is essential for understanding Indian society. A. M. Shah Joint family is changing, not disappearing. Verrier Elwin Tribes should develop according to their own culture.

castes improve status by adopting upper-caste practices."

sheets.text:
Social Stratification:

Forms of Social Stratification

Caste System

Features

• Birth-based

• Endogamy

• Occupation hereditary

• Restricted mobility

• Purity and pollution concept

Examples

• Brahmin

• Kshatriya

• Vaishya

• Shudra

Important Statement

G. S. Ghurye: "Caste is characterized by hierarchy, endogamy and social restrictions."

Class System

Features

• Based on wealth and occupation

• Achieved status

• Open system

• Social mobility possible

Examples

• Upper Class

• Middle Class

• Lower Class

Important Statement

Karl Marx: "History of all societies is the history of class struggle."

Estate System

Found in

• Medieval Europe

Estates

1\. Clergy 2. Nobility 3. Commoners

Slavery

Features

• Extreme inequality

• Person treated as property

• No freedom

Example

Ancient Greece, Rome, America

Traditional Basis

• Caste

• Varna

• Tribe

• Religion

Modern Basis

• Education

• Occupation

• Income

• Political Power

• Urbanization

Movement of individuals from one social position to another.

Intergenerational Mobility Between Generations

Intragenerational Mobility Within Lifetime

Example

Farmer's son becoming IAS Officer → Upward Mobility

sheets.heading: Functions of Family:
sheets.text:
Functions of Family:

Biological Functions

A. Reproduction

• Ensures continuity of society.

• Produces the next generation.

B. Regulation of Sexual Behaviour

• Provides socially approved sexual relations.

• Prevents social disorder.

C. Care and Protection

• Protects infants, children, elderly, and sick members.

Keywords

✔ Reproduction ✔ Continuity of society ✔ Sexual regulation

Social Functions

A. Socialization

• Family is the first school of the child.

• Teaches language, customs, values, traditions, and norms.

B. Social Control

• Encourages acceptable behaviour.

• Discourages deviant behaviour.

C. Social Identity

• Provides caste, religion, language, nationality, and status.

D. Transmission of Culture

• Transfers traditions from one generation to another.

Keywords

✔ Socialization ✔ Culture ✔ Values ✔ Norms

Economic Functions

A. Economic Security

• Provides food, shelter, clothing.

B. Division of Labour

• Members perform different roles.

C. Inheritance of Property

• Transfer of wealth and property.

D. Consumption Unit

• Family consumes goods and services collectively.

Keywords

✔ Economic support ✔ Property inheritance ✔ Resource sharing

Psychological Functions

A. Emotional Security

• Provides love, affection, care.

B. Personality Development

• Builds confidence and self-esteem.

C. Mental Support

• Helps members cope with stress and crises.

Keywords

✔ Love ✔ Affection ✔ Emotional stability

Educational Functions

• Family teaches basic education before school.

• Develops discipline and moral values.

• Encourages learning habits.

Example

A child learns:

• Language

• Manners

• Respect for elders

Religious Functions

• Introduces religious beliefs and rituals.

• Celebrates festivals and ceremonies.

• Preserves religious traditions.

Examples

• Diwali

• Eid

• Christmas

• Gurpurab

Protective Functions

• Protects members from social and economic risks.

• Supports children, women, elderly, and disabled persons.

Murdock's Four Universal Functions

According to George Peter Murdock:

Function Meaning Sexual Regulation of sexual relations Reproductive Birth of children Economic Economic cooperation Educational Socialization of children

sheets.heading: SOCIAL STABILITY:
sheets.text:
SOCIAL STABILITY:

Social Stability refers to the condition in which society maintains peace, order, harmony, continuity, and effective functioning of institutions despite social changes.

Key Features

• Social cohesion

• Social harmony

• Rule of law

• Economic security

• Political stability

• Inclusive development

Factors promoting Social Stability

• Family as primary agent of socialization

• Education and value inculcation

• Constitutional values

• Democratic institutions

• Welfare schemes and social justice measures

• Religious and cultural tolerance

Factors threatening Social Stability

• Poverty and unemployment

• Casteism

• Communalism

• Regionalism

• Extremism and terrorism

• Social inequality

• Gender discrimination

sheets.heading: KARL MARX (1818–1883):
sheets.text:
KARL MARX (1818–1883):

Karl Marx is known as the Father of Scientific Socialism and one of the most influential sociologists in conflict theory.

Important Works

• Das Kapital (1867)

• Communist Manifesto (1848) – with Friedrich Engels

Major Concepts

Historical Materialism

• Economic conditions shape society, politics, and culture.

Class Struggle

History is the history of class conflicts.

⇒ Examples:

• Master vs Slave

• Lord vs Serf

• Bourgeoisie vs Proletariat

Surplus Value

• Workers produce more value than the wages they receive.

Alienation

⇒ Workers become alienated from:

• Product of labour

• Production process

• Society

• Themselves

Revolution

• Marx predicted that workers would overthrow capitalism and establish a classless society.

sheets.heading: EMILE DURKHEIM (1858–1917)
sheets.text:
EMILE DURKHEIM (1858–1917)

Emile Durkheim is regarded as the Father of Modern Sociology.

Important Works

• The Division of Labour in Society

• Suicide

• Rules of Sociological Method

Major Concepts

Social Facts

Social facts are external forces that influence individual behaviour.

Examples:

• Laws

• Customs

• Religion

• Traditions

Collective Conscience

Shared beliefs and values that unite society.

Anomie

A condition of normlessness caused by rapid social change.

Examples:

• Crime

• Suicide

• Social unrest

sheets.heading: AUGUSTE COMTE (1798–1857):
sheets.text:
AUGUSTE COMTE (1798–1857):

Auguste Comte is known as the Father of Sociology.

Contribution

• Coined the term Sociology

• Founder of Positivism

Law of Three Stages

Theological Stage

Events explained through divine or supernatural forces.

Example: Rain occurs because of God's will.

Metaphysical Stage

Events explained through abstract concepts.

Example: Rain occurs because of nature's force.

Positive Stage

Events explained scientifically.

Example: Rain occurs due to atmospheric processes.

Positivism

Knowledge should be based on:

• Observation

• Experimentation

• Scientific evidence

Motto

"Order and Progress"

sheets.heading: MAX WEBER (1864–1920)
sheets.text:
MAX WEBER (1864–1920)

Max Weber is known as the Father of Interpretative Sociology.

Important Work

The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism

Major Concepts

Social Action

Instrumentally Rational Action

Goal-oriented behaviour.

Value Rational Action

Guided by values and ethics.

Traditional Action

Based on customs and traditions.

Affective Action

Based on emotions.

Ideal Type

An analytical model used to understand social reality.

Bureaucracy

Characteristics:

• Hierarchy

• Rules and regulations

• Specialization

• Merit system

• Impersonality

Types of Authority

Traditional Authority

Based on customs.

Charismatic Authority

Based on personality and leadership.

Legal-Rational Authority

Based on laws and rules.

sheets.heading: CASTE STATUS:
sheets.text:
CASTE STATUS:

Caste status refers to the social position occupied by an individual within the caste hierarchy.

Characteristics

• Determined by birth

• Fixed social position

• Linked with occupation

• Determines social prestige

Types of Status

Ascribed Status

Obtained by birth.

Examples:

• Caste

• Gender

• Family background

Achieved Status

Obtained through personal effort.

Examples:

• IAS Officer

• Doctor

• Scientist

Changes in Modern India

• Education

• Urbanization

• Industrialization

• Reservation policies

• Globalization

have increased achieved status.

sheets.heading: ENDOGAMY:
sheets.text:
ENDOGAMY:

Endogamy refers to marriage within one's own social group.

Examples

• Marriage within caste

• Marriage within tribe

• Marriage within religion

Features

• Preserves group identity

• Maintains caste boundaries

• Controls property transfer

Functions

• Cultural continuity

• Social solidarity

• Preservation of traditions

Related Concepts

Endogamy → Marriage within group

Exogamy → Marriage outside group

Hypergamy (Anuloma) → Marriage into higher caste

Hypogamy (Pratiloma) → Marriage into lower caste

sheets.heading: HEREDITARY:
sheets.text:
HEREDITARY:

Hereditary refers to characteristics, occupations, rights, or positions passed from one generation to another.

Examples

• Kingship

• Property ownership

• Traditional occupations

• Family businesses

Hereditary Occupation in Caste System

Examples:

• Potter

• Carpenter

• Blacksmith

• Weaver

Modern Changes

• Education

• Industrialization

• Urbanization

• Occupational mobility

have weakened hereditary occupations.

sheets.heading: SUCCESSION:
sheets.text:
SUCCESSION:

Succession refers to the transfer of authority, office, position, or property from one person to another.

Types

Lineal Succession

Transfer from parent to child.

Example: Father → Son

Collateral Succession

Transfer among relatives.

Example: Brother → Brother

Importance

• Continuity of institutions

• Political stability

• Social order

• Legitimacy

Examples

• Political leadership transition

• Royal succession

• Transfer of family property

sheets.heading: INHERITANCE:
sheets.text:
INHERITANCE:

Inheritance refers to the transfer of property, wealth, rights, and obligations from one generation to another after death.

Types of Inheritance:

Property Inheritance

⇒ Land, house, buildings

Financial Inheritance

⇒ Money, shares, savings

Cultural Inheritance

⇒ Language, customs, traditions

Social Inheritance

⇒ Status, reputation, networks

Important Laws

Hindu Succession Act, 1956

⇒ Provides inheritance rights to Hindus.

Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005

⇒ Granted daughters equal coparcenary rights.

Indian Succession Act, 1925

⇒ Applies mainly to Christians and others.

Muslim Personal Law

⇒ Inheritance governed by Sharia principles.

Contemporary Issues

• Women's property rights

• Gender equality

• Family disputes

• Property fragmentation

sheets.heading: INDOLOGICAL STUDY OF INDIAN SOCIETY:
sheets.text:
INDOLOGICAL STUDY OF INDIAN SOCIETY:

Indology is the study of Indian society through ancient texts, scriptures, epics, religious literature, and historical records.

Meaning

The Indological approach seeks to understand Indian society through:

• Vedas

• Upanishads

• Smritis

• Puranas

• Ramayana

• Mahabharata

• Dharmashastras

Major Scholars

G.S. Ghurye

⇒ Father of Indian Sociology.

Louis Dumont

⇒ Studied caste through religious and cultural texts.

K.M. Kapadia

⇒ Studied family and marriage systems.

Features

• Text-based approach

• Historical perspective

• Cultural interpretation

• Emphasis on continuity

sheets.heading: SOCIOLOGICAL IMAGINATION:
sheets.text:
SOCIOLOGICAL IMAGINATION:

Sociological Imagination is the ability to connect personal experiences with larger social forces and historical processes.

Introduced by

⇒ C. Wright Mills (1959)

Idea ⇒ Individual problems are often reflections of wider social issues.

Examples

Personal Trouble

⇒ A person is unemployed.

Public Issue

⇒ Large-scale unemployment due to economic slowdown.

Personal Trouble

⇒ Student stress.

Public Issue

⇒ Competitive education system.

sheets.heading: C. WRIGHT MILLS (1916–1962):
sheets.text:
C. WRIGHT MILLS (1916–1962):

American sociologist famous for the concept of Sociological Imagination.

Major Work

The Sociological Imagination (1959)

Key Contributions

Sociological Imagination

Understanding relationship between:

• Biography

• History

• Society

Power Elite Theory

Power is concentrated among:

• Political leaders

• Military leaders

• Corporate elites

Critique of Modern Society

Highlighted inequality and concentration of power.

sheets.heading: GEORGE SIMMEL (1858–1918):
sheets.text:
GEORGE SIMMEL (1858–1918):

German sociologist known for studying social interaction and urban life.

Major Contributions

Formal Sociology

⇒ Study of patterns of social interaction.

Social Interaction

⇒ Society exists because individuals interact.

Dyad and Triad

Dyad

Group of two people.

Example: Husband and wife

Triad

Group of three people.

Example: Teacher, parent, student

Metropolitan Life

Urbanization increases:

• Individualism

• Competition

• Social distance

sheets.heading: HERBERT BLUMER (1900–1987):
sheets.text:
HERBERT BLUMER (1900–1987):

American sociologist and founder of Symbolic Interactionism.

Major Contribution

Symbolic Interactionism

People act based on meanings they attach to things.

Meaning develops through:

• Social interaction

• Communication

• Interpretation

Examples

⇒ National Flag

Represents patriotism.

Wedding Ring

⇒ Represents marriage commitment.

Uniform ⇒ Represents authority.

Three Principles

Meaning

⇒ People act according to meanings.

Language

⇒ Language creates meaning.

Thought

⇒ Individuals interpret meanings.

sheets.heading: GENDER AUDITING:
sheets.text:
GENDER AUDITING:

Gender Audit is a systematic assessment of policies, programmes, institutions, and budgets to evaluate gender equality.

Objectives

• Promote gender justice

• Identify gender gaps

• Improve women's participation

• Ensure gender-sensitive governance

Components

• Gender budgeting

• Equal opportunities

• Workplace safety

• Decision-making participation

sheets.heading: NETWORK SOCIETY:
sheets.text:
NETWORK SOCIETY:

Network Society refers to a society where social, economic, political, and cultural activities are organized through digital networks.

Propounded By

Manuel Castells

Features

• Internet-based communication

• Global connectivity

• Information economy

• Digital platforms

• Virtual communities

Examples

• Social media networks

• Online education

• Digital governance

• E-commerce

sheets.heading: SOCIAL RESEARCH:
sheets.text:
SOCIAL RESEARCH:

Social Research is the systematic and scientific study of society, social relationships, and social problems.

Objectives

• Discover facts

• Explain social phenomena

• Test theories

• Solve social problems

Steps in Social Research

1\. Problem Identification 2. Literature Review 3. Hypothesis Formulation 4. Data Collection 5. Data Analysis 6. Interpretation 7. Report Writing

Types

• Basic Research

• Applied Research

• Quantitative Research

• Qualitative Research

sheets.heading: RELIGIOUS FUNDAMENTALISM:
sheets.text:
RELIGIOUS FUNDAMENTALISM:

Religious Fundamentalism refers to strict adherence to religious beliefs and practices, often rejecting modern interpretations.

Characteristics

• Literal interpretation of scriptures

• Religious conservatism

• Resistance to change

• Group exclusiveness

Causes

• Identity crisis

• Globalization

• Social insecurity

• Political mobilization

• Economic inequalities

sheets.heading: HIGH-RISK FAMILIES:
sheets.text:
HIGH-RISK FAMILIES:

High-risk families are families facing severe social, economic, health, psychological, or environmental challenges that adversely affect the well-being of family members.

Characteristics

• Poverty and unemployment

• Domestic violence

• Substance abuse

• Single-parent households

• Chronic illness or disability

• Child neglect and abuse

• Family conflicts

Causes

Economic Factors

• Poverty

• Debt burden

• Job insecurity

Social Factors

• Family breakdown

• Migration

• Social exclusion

Psychological Factors

• Mental stress

• Depression

• Addiction

Consequences

• Child labour

• School dropouts

• Juvenile delinquency

• Malnutrition

• Crime and deviance

Government Measures

• Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)

• Mission Vatsalya

• POSHAN Abhiyaan

• National Family Benefit Scheme

sheets.heading: GENDER MAINSTREAMING:
sheets.text:
GENDER MAINSTREAMING:

Gender Mainstreaming is the process of integrating gender perspectives into all policies, programmes, laws, and institutions to achieve gender equality.

Origin

Promoted globally during the Fourth World Conference on Women held in Beijing (1995).

Objectives

• Achieve gender equality

• Reduce gender discrimination

• Promote women's participation

• Ensure equitable development

Key Components

Gender Analysis

⇒ Assessment of gender impacts.

Gender Planning

⇒ Incorporating gender concerns in policymaking.

Gender Budgeting

⇒ Allocating resources for gender-sensitive programmes.

Gender Monitoring

⇒ Evaluating gender outcomes.

Importance

• Women's empowerment

• Inclusive governance

• Social justice

• Sustainable development

Examples

• Beti Bachao Beti Padhao

• Gender Budget Statements

• Mission Shakti

• Women Reservation initiatives

UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS (UDHR):

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is the foundational international document that recognizes fundamental rights and freedoms of all human beings.

Adoption

Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948.

Background

Prepared after the atrocities of World War II to safeguard human dignity.

Key Features

• Universal applicability

• Equality and non-discrimination

• Protection of civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights

• Human dignity at its core

Structure

• Preamble

• 30 Articles

Important Rights

Civil and Political Rights

• Right to life

• Freedom of speech

• Freedom of religion

• Equality before law

Economic and Social Rights

• Right to work

• Right to education

• Right to health

• Right to social security

Importance for India

• Influenced Fundamental Rights

• Inspired Directive Principles of State Policy

• Basis for human rights legislation

Related Institutions

United Nations (UN)

National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)

State Human Rights Commissions

sheets.heading: SOCIAL DIAGNOSIS:
sheets.text:
SOCIAL DIAGNOSIS:

Social Diagnosis is the systematic assessment of an individual's or group's social conditions, problems, and needs before planning interventions.

Introduced By

⇒ Mary Richmond

Meaning

⇒ Just as doctors diagnose diseases, social workers diagnose social problems.

Objectives

• Identify social problems

• Understand root causes

• Assess needs

• Plan interventions

Steps in Social Diagnosis

1\. Information Collection

⇒ Gather facts about the individual or family.

2\. Problem Identification

⇒ Identify social, economic, or psychological issues.

3\. Analysis

⇒ Determine causes and consequences.

4\. Planning

⇒ Develop intervention strategies.

5\. Follow-Up

⇒ Monitor outcomes.

Areas of Application

• Child welfare

• Family counselling

• Community development

• Rehabilitation services

• Poverty alleviation programmes

Importance

• Scientific problem-solving

• Effective social work

• Better policy implementation

• Targeted interventions

Example

A school dropout may be diagnosed as facing:

• Poverty

• Family conflict

• Child labour

• Lack of educational support

The intervention is then designed accordingly.

sheets.heading: Manu Smriti and Types of Hindu Marriages:
sheets.text:
Manu Smriti and Types of Hindu Marriages:

Eight Types of Marriages according to Manu Smriti

Type of Marriage Meaning Status in Manusmriti Brahma Marriage Daughter given to a learned and worthy groom Approved Daiva Marriage Daughter given to a priest performing sacrifice Approved Arsha Marriage Marriage bull) after receiving symbolic gifts (cow and

Approved

Prajapatya Marriage Marriage based on duty and family life Approved Gandharva Marriage Marriage by mutual love and consent Conditionally

Accepted Asura Marriage Bride purchased by giving wealth to family Disapproved Rakshasa Marriage Marriage by force/abduction after battle Disapproved Paisacha Marriage Marriage woman through deceit or exploitation of

Most Condemned

1\. Brahma Marriage

Meaning

Father voluntarily gives his daughter to a qualified, educated, and virtuous groom.

Features

• No dowry or bride price

• Groom is knowledgeable in Vedas

• Highest form of marriage

Modern Equivalent

Arranged marriage based on qualifications and compatibility.

2\. Daiva Marriage

Meaning

Daughter is given to a priest (Ritvik) who officiates a sacrifice.

Features

• Linked with religious rituals

• Groom is a priest

3\. Arsha Marriage

Meaning

Marriage performed after receiving a symbolic gift such as a cow and a bull from the groom.

Features

• Symbolic exchange only

• Common among sages and hermits

4\. Prajapatya Marriage

Meaning

Marriage performed with blessings emphasizing duty, family welfare, and procreation.

Features

• Focus on Dharma

• Husband and wife share responsibilities

5\. Gandharva Marriage

Meaning

Marriage based on mutual love and consent of the couple.

Features

• No parental approval necessary

• Love marriage

• Voluntary union

Examples

• Shakuntala and Dushyanta

• Many references in epics

6\. Asura Marriage

Meaning

Marriage where the groom gives wealth to the bride's family and "purchases" the bride.

Features

• Bride price involved

• Wealth becomes primary consideration

7\. Rakshasa Marriage

Meaning

Marriage through forceful abduction of a woman.

Features

• Associated with Kshatriyas

• Occurs after warfare or conflict

Example

Abduction-type marriages mentioned in epics.

8\. Paisacha Marriage

Meaning

Marriage involving deceit, intoxication, coercion, or exploitation of a woman without her consent.

Features

• Most condemned form

• Considered immoral and sinful

Approved (Prashasta) Marriages

1\. Brahma 2. Daiva 3. Arsha 4. Prajapatya

Disapproved (Aprashasta) Marriages

5\. Gandharva 6. Asura 7. Rakshasa 8. Paisacha
